text:
This chapter covers how to judge fruit ripeness and the practical methods for harvesting jackfruit. The text emphasizes that, unlike some fruits, jackfruit does not ripen further in a way that fully compensates for being picked too early — fruit picked significantly under-ripe will not develop full sweetness and flavor — so correctly judging ripeness at harvest is important for fruit quality. Visual and other sensory cues described in the source for judging ripeness include changes in rind color (the spines/rind becoming a duller, more yellow-brown color as the fruit ripens rather than staying bright green), a hollow sound when the fruit is tapped, a change in the fruit's smell (ripe fruit developing the characteristic strong jackfruit aroma), and the spines on the rind spreading further apart and softening slightly as the fruit approaches full ripeness.

The chapter gives an approximate timeframe from fruit set to ripeness (on the order of a few months, consistent with the timing discussion in earlier chapters) and discusses harvest technique: because ripe fruit is heavy and produces a sticky latex when cut from the stem, growers are advised to cut the fruit stalk carefully (rather than letting the fruit fall, which can damage it), often lowering large fruit by rope or with assistance rather than dropping it, and to handle cut fruit carefully afterward to avoid bruising before sale or processing.

The chapter also briefly discusses staggering harvest of individual fruits on the same tree according to their individual ripeness (rather than harvesting an entire tree's fruit set at once), consistent with the extended-harvest strategies discussed in the previous chapter, and notes that fruit intended for distant markets should generally be harvested slightly less ripe than fruit intended for immediate local sale or home consumption, to allow for transport time.
